description:
I'm tackling the Be An Earth System Trend Detective! challenge and looking to build a balanced team.

I’ll handle the quantitative core: cleaning NASA time-series datasets, running statistical trend tests (Python/R), and generating insights.

Looking for 1–2 teammates with web/UI skills or storytelling experience to help build a sleek dashboard (e.g.,Streamlit) and craft a pitch deck. Let's build a clean, data-backed MVP together! Reach out if you're interested.
summary:
EcoLens turns NASA Earth-science data into investigations that a student can follow. Pick any place on Earth: a city, a pair of coordinates or a click on a 3D globe. EcoLens fetches 31 Earth-system variables from NASA POWER (monthly, 1981–2025), tests each one for a trend, and answers the four questions the challenge asks: What is changing, Where, By how much, and Whether the change is statistically significant. A trend is called "significant" only when
two independent tests agree, a least-squares t-test and the Mann-Kendall test, at α = 0.05.
EcoLens then ranks every variable at that place with a correction for multiple testing, compares the measurement with a second independent record where one exists, shows the year the trend
became significant, and puts it next to what CMIP6 climate models project for 2041–2060. Every case ends with what the analysis cannot tell you. It matters because the same variable can rise one place and fall a short distance away, and a slope through noisy data is not a trend until it has been tested. EcoLens makes that test visible, explains it in plain words, and is open to anyone with a browser.
details:
What it does and how it works EcoLens turns raw NASA Earth-science data into simple, local climate investigations.You pick any city, coordinate, or spot on a 3D globe, and the app fetches 31 Earth-system variables from NASA POWER (spanning 1981–2025). It runs two independent statistical tests (a least-squares t-test and a Mann-Kendall test) to separate real long-term trends from natural year-to-year noise. From there, it ranks which variables are changing fastest at that spot, shows the exact year a trend became statistically significant, cross-checks the data against independent records (like NASA GISTEMP and NOAA weather stations), and compares past trends to 2050 climate model projections (CMIP6).

Benefits

  • Accessible: You start with a place on a map rather than digging through complex data portals or obscure variable codes.
  • Plain-English translation: Every statistical verdict is explained in simple, rule-based language, with the underlying numbers one click away.
  • Free and frictionless: Open-source, runs in any browser, and requires no login.

Intended impact Built for high school and college students—as well as anyone curious about their local environment—EcoLens teaches critical scientific habits. Instead of blindly trusting a trend line, users learn to test for statistical significance, check a second source, and understand the limits of what data can actually prove. Because the statistical engine is decoupled from the interface, educators or developers can also easily plug in new datasets later.

Tools and tech stack

  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, NumPy, and SciPy (using NASA POWER as the live data source, plus pre-processed static layers from GISTEMP, MODIS, and CMIP6).
  • Frontend: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Three.js (react-three-fiber) for the 3D globe, and Recharts for data visualization.
  • Hosting: Deployed on Vercel.

How it is creative We framed climate data analysis like a detective investigation. Features like "When the case cracked" (pinpointing the exact year a trend crossed the threshold into statistical significance), "Witnesses" (cross-examining independent datasets), and "Opposite twins" (finding the closest nearby grid cells trending in completely opposite directions) turn dry statistics into a visual, intuitive story.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific honesty: We required two independent statistical tests to agree before calling a trend "significant," corrected for autocorrelation and multiple testing, avoided AI-generated text in the verdicts to prevent hallucinations, and explicitly listed the limitations of every single result.
  • Accessibility: We designed the app with full keyboard navigation, screen-reader alternatives for the 3D globe, raw data tables behind every chart, and reduced-motion support so anyone can use it.
